source.title: A Good Place to Lose Your Mind

primary.axis: every distractor that restores symmetry is tempting and wrong

tension_system.interaction: the secondary tension complicates the primary at the passage's turn

family_realization.note: Memory and anticipation become genuinely asymmetric; praise and blame appear, but receive limited development and weaker cascading consequences.

ending_behavior.note: The blue box returns as unequal permissions; the qualified ending holds rather than merely summarizing.

voice_consistency.note: Formal irony and the blue-box detail sustain voice, though recurrent abstract openings create some generic essay texture.

distractor_efficiency.note: Most questions offer plausible traps—symmetry, stage confusion, scope inflation, adjacent answers—without relying chiefly on lexical extremity.

explanation_quality.note: Explanations generally identify mechanisms and passage locations, especially analogy, trusteeship, absent claimants, and paragraph removal.

answers.reasoning: The passage rejects symmetry between past and future claims, defining commonweal through unequal duties and permissions.
The central distinction rests on future persons being unable to contest policies; this would collapse that asymmetry.
The ordered petitions illustrate how remembrance and recorded injury can seem to grant moral standing.
The passage explicitly says later generations are asked to treat remembrance and anticipation as matching duties.
That paragraph explains differing warrants: memory recognizes an injured claimant, while anticipation governs uncontestable future conditions.
The author presents trustees for posterity and proxies for the past as an attractive rival position, not his conclusion.
The passage insists future claimants cannot contest or authorize representation before policies govern their lives.
The initial analogy fails because ceremonial kinship between claims does not establish reciprocal political authority.
